sub: English idioms borrow from sports and school all the time — 'hit the books,' 'drop the ball.' Read the clues, compare them across languages, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms sports school study ball hit the books drop the ball ballpark figure the ball is in your court english spanish pelota figurative language multilingual esl grade 6 7 8

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Name the source and the meaning
brief.p: You are reading idioms as figurative language — noticing HOW the phrase works, not whether the words are literally true. Find the meaning, use context, and compare across languages.

win.p: You separated the literal picture from the real meaning and compared languages. Noticing how figurative language works is a powerful reading skill.

clues.title: 'Hit the books'
clues.body: 'Hit the books' means to study hard — you don't actually hit anything. Spanish says 'ponerse a estudiar' or 'hincar los codos' (dig in the elbows) — a different picture, same idea.

clues.title: 'A ballpark figure'
clues.body: A 'ballpark figure' is a rough estimate, not an exact number. It comes from baseball. Spanish says 'una cifra aproximada' — no sports picture at all.

clues.title: 'Drop the ball'
clues.body: To 'drop the ball' means to make a mistake or fail a responsibility. Spanish says 'meter la pata' (put in the paw/foot) — a different picture, same idea: to mess up.

clues.title: 'The ball is in your court'
clues.body: 'The ball is in your court' means it is your turn to decide or act. Spanish says 'la pelota está en tu tejado' (the ball is on your roof) — the SAME ball, a different place.

clues.title: Same words, two meanings
clues.body: Watch out — some of these can be literal too. You can really 'drop the ball' in a game, or figuratively fail a task. The sentence around the phrase (the context) tells you which meaning is meant. Strong readers let context decide.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The largest stadium in the world holds about 114,000 people. That is a true sports fact — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: Read it in context
locks.q: Read the sentence: 'Everyone was counting on Marco, but he dropped the ball and forgot to submit the form.' What does 'dropped the ball' mean HERE?
options: He failed to do his part
He handed the job to a teammate
He changed the plan at the last minute
locks.reason: The context — forgetting to submit the form — shows Marco failed his responsibility. The other options sound reasonable, but the sentence doesn't support them, and no real ball was dropped: it's figurative.

locks.title: Which rules are really true?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE about how idioms work. One only SOUNDS true — leave it out.

items.t: You can't find an idiom's meaning by translating its words one by one
The same idea can use a different image in another language — 'drop the ball' vs. Spanish 'meter la pata'
The same phrase can be literal or figurative depending on the sentence around it
If English and Spanish use the same word in an idiom, the idiom must mean the same in both

locks.reason: The last statement only sounds true: sharing a word does NOT guarantee the idiom matches. The other three are the real rules for reading idioms in context.

locks.title: Follow two idioms
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes a coherent apology — using BOTH 'drop the ball' and 'the ball is in your court.'

pads.e: ✅ 'This time I finished my part and sent it over.'
😬 'I know I dropped the ball on the last project.'
🎾 'So now the ball is in your court.'

locks.reason: The order builds a mini-story: admit a past failure ('dropped the ball'), do the work this time, then hand it off ('the ball is in your court'). Tracking two idioms across a passage is real reading.

locks.title: Name the source
locks.q: These idioms borrow their pictures from two everyday areas of life (think 'hit the books,' 'ballpark figure,' 'the ball is in your court'). Name ONE of those two areas in one word.
locks.reason: The idioms come from SPORTS ('ballpark,' 'drop the ball,' 'ball in your court') and SCHOOL ('hit the books'). Spotting an idiom's source domain — where its picture comes from — is a strong analytical move.

h1: Time & Money: Idioms That Cost You
sub: English treats time and money like objects — 'time flies,' 'break the bank.' Read the clues, compare them across languages, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms time money break the bank time flies once in a blue moon el tiempo vuela save time waste time english spanish metaphor figurative language multilingual esl grade 7 8

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Read time and money as metaphors
brief.p: English often treats time and money as if they were objects you can save, spend, or lose. Notice the metaphor, find the meaning, and compare across languages.

win.p: You read time and money as metaphors, found the meanings, and compared languages — strong figurative-language thinking.

clues.title: 'Time flies'
clues.body: 'Time flies' means time passes very quickly. Spanish says 'el tiempo vuela' (time flies) — the SAME picture: flying time!

clues.title: 'Break the bank'
clues.body: To 'break the bank' means to cost too much or use up all your money. Spanish says 'costar un dineral' (to cost a fortune) — a different picture, same idea: very expensive.

clues.title: 'Once in a blue moon'
clues.body: 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely. Spanish says 'de vez en cuando' (from time to time) or 'de Pascuas a Ramos' — a different picture, same idea: rarely.

clues.title: Time acts like money
clues.body: In English you can 'save time,' 'spend time,' or 'waste time' — as if time were money. Spanish does this too: 'ahorrar tiempo' (save time), 'perder el tiempo' (waste time).

clues.title: A false-friend warning
clues.body: Careful with word-for-word guesses. 'Break the bank' is NOT 'romper el banco' in Spanish, and 'once in a blue moon' has nothing to do with a real blue moon. Idioms almost never translate literally — you learn them as whole phrases.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Diamonds are the hardest natural material on Earth. That is a true science fact — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: Read it in context
locks.q: Read: 'Don't worry — this trip won't break the bank.' What does 'break the bank' mean HERE?
options: It won't cost too much money
locks.reason: The context ('won't…') tells you it's about money — the trip won't cost too much. The distractors describe OTHER idioms (about time or difficulty), not this one.

locks.title: Which rules are really true?
locks.q: Check every TRUE statement. One overgeneralizes from a single example — leave it out.

items.t: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words
English 'time flies' and Spanish 'el tiempo vuela' happen to use the SAME image
Most idioms cannot be translated word for word into another language
Because 'time flies' matches in both languages, all idioms will match between English and Spanish

locks.reason: The false statement overgeneralizes from one lucky match — 'time flies' matching does NOT mean every idiom matches. Reasoning from one example to 'all' is the trap.

locks.title: Follow two idioms
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes sense — using BOTH 'time flies' and 'once in a blue moon.'

pads.e: 🌙 'We only get together once in a blue moon.'
👋 'I can't believe a whole year has passed — time flies!'
📅 'Let's not wait so long next time.'

locks.reason: The order builds a thought: time passed fast ('time flies'), they rarely meet ('once in a blue moon'), so they should plan sooner. Tracking two idioms across a passage is real reading.

locks.title: Name the hidden comparison
locks.q: In these idioms, time is treated like one other thing you can 'save,' 'spend,' or 'waste.' Type that one thing (one word).
locks.reason: English treats TIME like MONEY — you save it, spend it, or waste it. Naming that hidden comparison (a conceptual metaphor) is sophisticated figurative-language thinking.
